title: The Modern Church and the Global Shift
subtitle: The fundamentalist and modernist split, the churches under the dictators, Barmen and Bonhoeffer, the fire from Azusa Street, and the great reversal that moved the faith's center south.

sections.title: The Century Nobody Predicted
sections.body:
In 1900, better than four of every five Christians in the world lived in Europe or North America, and the sober expectation of the age was that the twentieth century would extend the pattern. Christian civilization, as the West did not blush to call itself, would spread with its railways and its schools until the map was finished. Almost nothing in that expectation survived. The century that followed gave the church two world wars hatched in Christian Europe, the most systematic persecutions in its history, the emptying of the very pews that had sent the missionaries, and, at the same time, the largest and fastest expansion of Christian faith ever recorded, almost none of it where the strategists expected.

No one at the great mission conference of 1910 predicted that within a lifetime the heartlands of the faith would be shifting to Africa, Asia, and Latin America. No one predicted that Christianity's deadliest enemies in the new century would not be rival religions but ideologies born inside Christendom itself, fascism and communism, each demanding the worship the church owed to Christ. And few would have guessed that the century's most consequential revival was already beginning in a shabby building in Los Angeles under a one-eyed black preacher.

This is the century that made the world the reader lives in, and it ends on the fact every Western believer now has to sit with. The average Christian today is not a Westerner. How that happened is the story of this essay, and it begins with the Western church tearing itself in half.

sections.title: Fundamentalists and Modernists
sections.body:
The Western argument of the early century was about whether Christianity could survive modern knowledge, and it split American Protestantism down the middle. On one side stood the modernists, heirs of a century of critical scholarship, who believed the faith would die among educated people unless it made peace with Darwin and the historians. They were not villains. They were trying to save Christianity's credibility, and some of them carried honest doubts their grandparents never had to face. On the other side stood those who answered that a faith adjusted to fit each new consensus was not being saved but dissolved. Between 1910 and 1915, two California oil men financed The Fundamentals, twelve volumes defending the faith's foundations, mailed free to Christian workers by the hundreds of thousands, and the movement had a name.

The battle had famous set pieces. In 1922 Harry Emerson Fosdick preached his New York sermon asking whether the fundamentalists should win, and in 1923 the Princeton scholar J. Gresham Machen answered with a book arguing that consistent liberalism was not a purified Christianity but a different religion altogether. Each man deserves to be heard at his strongest, and each accused the other of losing the actual faith. In 1925 the state of Tennessee tried a schoolteacher for teaching evolution, and the fundamentalists won the verdict and lost the press, the universities, and the cultural high ground for two generations. William Jennings Bryan, their champion, died in his sleep five days after the trial ended.

The losing side did not disappear. It built colleges, radio networks, and mission boards, and at midcentury re-emerged, chastened and organized, as the evangelicalism of Billy Graham's generation. The argument itself never ended. It is running in your church now, under new names.

sections.title: Barmen and the German Failure
sections.body:
When Hitler took power in 1933, most German Protestants welcomed him. That sentence should be allowed to hurt. A movement calling itself the German Christians set out to merge church and regime, complete with a church adoption of the state's racial exclusions, so that a pastor of Jewish descent could be barred from a German pulpit. Against this, a minority gathered at Barmen in May of 1934 and issued a declaration, drafted chiefly by Karl Barth, whose first thesis every church under pressure has reached for since. Jesus Christ, as attested in Scripture, is the one Word of God whom the church must hear, trust, and obey, in life and in death, and the church rejects as false doctrine the claim that other events, powers, figures, or truths could stand beside him as God's revelation.

It was a brave document, and we should be honest about its limits. Barmen defended the church's freedom from the state. It said nothing directly about the persecution of the Jews, and most of its signers never did either. The Confessing Church it created was a resisting minority inside a largely accommodating church, and its bravest members went to prison. Martin Niemoller, a U-boat captain turned pastor who had at first welcomed the regime, learned what it was, said so from his pulpit, and spent seven years in the camps as Hitler's personal prisoner.

In October of 1945 the surviving leaders published the Stuttgart Declaration, confessing that they had not been courageous enough, had not prayed or believed or loved enough. Churches rarely say such things out loud. It was the truest sentence German Protestantism produced in the whole era, and it came too late for six million people.

sections.title: Bonhoeffer
sections.body:
Dietrich Bonhoeffer was twenty-seven when Hitler came to power, a brilliant Berlin theologian who saw the disease early and named it. He helped lead the Confessing Church's illegal seminary at Finkenwalde until the Gestapo closed it in 1937, and out of that community came the two small books, Discipleship and Life Together, that keep his name alive in ordinary congregations. Cheap grace, he wrote there, is the deadly enemy of the church, forgiveness preached without repentance, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross.

In the summer of 1939, safe in New York with a teaching post and every reason to stay, he sailed home within the month, writing to a friend that he would have no right to help rebuild Christian life in Germany after the war unless he shared its trials now. The decision killed him. Drawn by his family into the conspiracy against Hitler, he was arrested in April of 1943, and on the ninth of April 1945, in the concentration camp at Flossenburg, weeks before the war's end, he was hanged with his fellow conspirators. The camp doctor, who did not know who he was, wrote years later that in fifty years of medicine he had hardly ever seen a man go to his death so composed and so given over to God.

His story is told too often as a lone hero's, which he would have hated. He belongs inside the German church's failure, as its exception and therefore its accusation. The German church produced one Bonhoeffer and a great silence, and the silence is what made him necessary. Every church since that has faced a state demanding worship has had to decide which of the two it will add to.

sections.title: The Churches Under Communism
sections.body:
What Germany did to the church in a decade, the Soviet Union attempted for seventy years. The Bolsheviks inherited a society saturated in Orthodox Christianity and set out to abolish faith itself. Churches were dynamited, Moscow's great Cathedral of Christ the Saviour among them in 1931, with a public swimming pool eventually built in the pit. In the purge years of the late 1930s, Orthodox clergy were shot by the tens of thousands, and of the tens of thousands of parishes open before the revolution, only a few hundred still functioned legally by 1939. Then came the strange evidence. The regime's own census of 1937 asked about belief, and more than half the population, knowing the risk, still declared itself religious. The census officials were purged and the results suppressed. The cathedral, for the record, has been rebuilt. The state that dynamited it no longer exists.

China ran the experiment even harder. The missionaries were expelled by 1952, and in the Cultural Revolution public worship was extinguished entirely. When the churches reopened after 1979, the world discovered that the church had not died underground. It had multiplied, into the tens of millions by every serious estimate, though no census can settle the number, and it keeps growing under a pressure that has never fully lifted.

By many reckonings, more Christians died for their faith in the twentieth century than in any century before it. The counting is disputed. The scale is not. The century the West remembers as the age of doubt was, for much of the world's church, the age of martyrs, and the two stories were happening at the same time, largely unknown to each other.

sections.title: Azusa Street and the Rising South
sections.body:
In April of 1906, in a former stable on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a revival broke out under William Seymour, a preacher blind in one eye, the son of freed slaves. The city's newspapers mocked the meetings. The meetings did not care. Black, white, and immigrant believers worshiped together in a Jim Crow decade, and one participant marveled that the color line was washed away in the blood. From that unpromising room, Pentecostalism spread along shipping routes and mission networks until, a century later, the wider Pentecostal and charismatic family numbered somewhere over half a billion people by common estimates, perhaps the largest Christian movement since the Reformation. It started with the people the culture counted last.

The global South was already stirring on its own. In the Congo in 1921, a Baptist catechist named Simon Kimbangu preached and healed for a few months before Belgium jailed him for the remaining thirty years of his life. The church his followers built now counts its members in the millions. The East African Revival renewed whole regions from the 1930s. A revival in Pyongyang in 1907 set Korean Protestantism on a course that would one day make South Korea a major missionary-sending nation. Catholicism turned its face the same direction. The Second Vatican Council, meeting from 1962 to 1965, put worship into the world's languages, and within two generations the church's demographic heart had moved so far south that a Latin American pope surprised no one who had been counting.

In 1974, at Billy Graham's global congress in Lausanne, Latin American theologians stood up and told Western evangelicals that discipleship could not be separated from justice, and the daughter churches began, audibly, to teach the parents.

sections.title: The Average Christian Is Not a Westerner
sections.body:
Sometime around 1980 the balance tipped. For the first time since the Middle Ages, most of the world's Christians were not Europeans or North Americans, and the gap has widened since. Perhaps ten million Africans were Christians in 1900. By the century's end, the standard estimates said more than three hundred million, and the number has kept climbing. The historian Philip Jenkins put the new reality in a sentence. If you want to picture a typical Christian now, he suggested, picture a woman in a village in Nigeria or a Brazilian favela. Meanwhile the old heartlands emptied. Lesslie Newbigin, coming home to England in 1974 after decades as a missionary bishop in India, found the sending country stranger to the gospel than the one he had left, and spent his last years asking in print whether the West itself could be converted. The traffic reversed. Some of the largest congregations in Europe's capitals are now led by African pastors, missionaries to the continent that once sent missionaries to them.

None of this makes the southern churches a finished product. They wrestle with prosperity preachers, with syncretism, with persecution, with the same tribal temptations every church inherits. They are not the church's future perfected. They are simply the church.

The historian Andrew Walls saw the pattern underneath it all. Christianity has no permanent capital. Its heartlands advance and recede in series, Jerusalem to the Greek cities to Rome to the northern barbarians to the Atlantic world, each center in its turn becoming a mission field, each margin a center. The faith that began in a borrowed room in Jerusalem has never yet stayed where it was put. The Western church is not the story's owner. It never was. It is one more province of a kingdom that keeps its capital elsewhere.

keyFigures.name: William Seymour
keyFigures.note: Son of freed slaves whose Azusa Street revival began the Pentecostal movement.

keyFigures.name: Karl Barth
keyFigures.note: Swiss theologian and principal drafter of the Barmen Declaration of 1934.

keyFigures.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
keyFigures.note: Theologian of the Confessing Church, hanged at Flossenburg in April 1945.

keyFigures.name: Martin Niemoller
keyFigures.note: Pastor who welcomed the regime, resisted it, and spent seven years in the camps.

keyFigures.name: Simon Kimbangu
keyFigures.note: Congolese catechist, jailed for thirty years, whose movement became a church of millions.

keyFigures.name: Lesslie Newbigin
keyFigures.note: Missionary bishop in India who returned to ask whether the West could be converted.

keyFigures.name: Billy Graham
keyFigures.note: Evangelist of the postwar re-emergence, whose Lausanne congress gathered the world church.
